description: Force and pressure - what a force does, contact and non-contact forces, and why pressure depends on area.

slides.heading: What is a force?
bullets: A push or a pull on an object.
A force has both size and direction.
Forces are measured in newtons (N).
Two or more forces can add up or cancel out.
slides.notes: Push a desk one way, then have a student push the other way - show forces in opposite directions.

slides.heading: What a force can do
bullets: Make a still object start moving.
Make a moving object speed up, slow down or stop.
Change the direction of motion.
Change the shape of an object.
slides.notes: Demonstrate with a ball roll, a catch, and squeezing a piece of dough or a sponge.

slides.heading: Contact and non-contact forces
bullets: Contact force - acts only by touching: muscular force, friction.
Non-contact force - acts from a distance.
Magnetic force - between magnets and magnetic materials.
Gravitational force - pulls every object towards the Earth.
slides.notes: Drop a chalk piece (gravity, non-contact) and lift a book (muscular, contact).

slides.heading: What is pressure?
bullets: Pressure = force divided by the area it acts on.
Same force on a smaller area gives more pressure.
Same force on a larger area gives less pressure.
Measured in newtons per square metre (pascal).
slides.notes: Press a pencil between two fingers - the sharp tip hurts more though the force is equal.

slides.heading: Pressure in everyday life
bullets: Knives and needles are sharp to raise pressure and cut easily.
School bags have wide straps to lower pressure on the shoulder.
A tractor has wide tyres so it does not sink in soft soil.
Nails are pointed; hammers are broad.
slides.notes: Ask students for two more examples of shapes designed to raise or lower pressure.

slides.heading: Pressure by liquids and gases
bullets: Liquids press on the walls and bottom of their container.
Liquid pressure increases with depth.
Gases also exert pressure in all directions - like air in a balloon.
The atmosphere presses on us from all sides.
slides.notes: A tin with holes at different heights squirts water farther from the lower holes - deeper means more pressure.

slides.heading: Quick recap
bullets: Force is a push or pull; it changes motion or shape.
Contact forces need touching; gravity and magnetism act at a distance.
Pressure = force / area.
Small area -> high pressure; large area -> low pressure.
slides.notes: Four students, one point each, to close the lesson.
